summary: This document specifies procedures for BGP MPLS-based Ethernet VPNs (EVPN), which let service providers offer Layer 2 Ethernet connectivity between customer sites using BGP to distribute MAC address information. It meets the requirements set out in RFC 7209.

plainLanguage.summary: A company has offices in different cities. This lets a provider make them look like they share one big office network, using a routing system to share who is where.

questions: what are the evpn route types
how does evpn learn mac addresses
subtitle: How providers use BGP and MPLS to stitch customer Ethernet sites together, with multihoming and MAC learning done in the control plane.

tldr.problem: VPLS, the older way to offer Layer 2 VPNs, struggles with multihoming and redundancy, multicast optimization, provisioning simplicity, flow-based load balancing and multipathing, which matter in data centers.
tldr.mechanism: EVPN has provider edge routers advertise the MAC addresses they learn from customers, and the Ethernet segments they attach to, in Multiprotocol BGP using a new EVPN NLRI with four route types. Other routers use those routes to forward, load balance and fail over.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7432 is a Proposed Standard that meets the requirements of RFC 7209. It has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 8584, RFC 9161, RFC 9572, RFC 9573 and RFC 9746.

today: RFC 7432 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 8584, RFC 9161, RFC 9572, RFC 9573 and RFC 9746. Read it together with those updates.

sections.title: Why EVPN Exists
sections.content:
Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) is described in the RFC as a proven and widely deployed technology. It has limits, though, in multihoming and redundancy, multicast optimization, provisioning simplicity, flow-based load balancing and multipathing. These limits matter most for Data Center deployments. RFC 7209 sets out the motivation and requirements, and this document defines procedures that meet them.

An EVPN instance (EVI) connects Customer Edge devices (CEs) to Provider Edge devices (PEs) at the edge of the MPLS infrastructure. A CE can be a host, a router or a switch. The PEs provide virtual Layer 2 bridged connectivity between the CEs. The PEs can be linked by MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs) or by an IP infrastructure using IP/GRE or other IP tunneling, but the detailed procedures are specified only for MPLS LSPs.

The main change from VPLS is where MAC addresses are learned. Between PEs, learning happens in the control plane using Multiprotocol BGP rather than in the data plane. A PE advertises the MAC addresses it learns from its CEs, together with an MPLS label, to the other PEs. This gives more control over who learns what, allows policies, and enables load balancing to and from CEs that are multihomed to several PEs. Between a PE and a CE, learning uses whatever method suits the CE.

The policy attributes are very similar to IP VPNs. An EVPN instance needs a Route Distinguisher (RD) that is unique per MAC-VRF and one or more globally unique Route Targets (RTs).
sections.plainLanguage: The old way made every router shout to find out where each computer lived. EVPN has the routers write down who lives where and pass the list around, which is quicker and lets a customer plug into two routers at once.

sections.title: Ethernet Segments and Ethernet Tags
sections.content:
When a customer site connects to one or more PEs through a set of Ethernet links, that set of links is an Ethernet segment (ES). Each multihomed segment gets a unique non-zero Ethernet Segment Identifier (ESI), a 10-octet value. ESI 0 means a single-homed site, and ESI 0xFF repeated 10 times is the reserved MAX-ESI. The ESI SHOULD be unique network wide. If the CEs are not managed by the operator, the operator MUST configure a network-wide unique ESI for the segment.

The first octet of the ESI is a type, and the remaining 9 octets are the value. Types 1 and 2 are generated automatically from LACP and from spanning tree BPDUs; types 3, 4 and 5 are built from a system MAC address, a router ID or an AS number plus a local discriminator.

An Ethernet Tag ID is a 32-bit field containing a 12-bit or 24-bit identifier for a particular broadcast domain, such as a VLAN, within an EVPN instance. The value 0xFFFFFFFF is reserved as MAX-ET. How the tag is used depends on the service interface. In a VLAN-based service one VLAN maps to one MAC-VRF. In a VLAN bundle service several VLANs share one bridge table, so MAC addresses MUST be unique across those VLANs and VLAN ID translation is not allowed. In a VLAN-aware bundle service each VLAN has its own bridge table inside one MAC-VRF.
sections.plainLanguage: A customer's cable to the provider can be a pair of cables going to two different routers. The pair gets one name tag so everyone knows they belong together. A VLAN is like a separate classroom on the same network.

sections.title: The BGP EVPN Routes
sections.content:
EVPN defines a new BGP Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) called the EVPN NLRI. It starts with a 1-octet Route Type and a 1-octet Length, followed by data specific to the route type. It is carried in BGP using Multiprotocol Extensions with Address Family Identifier (AFI) 25 (L2VPN) and Subsequent Address Family Identifier (SAFI) 70 (EVPN). BGP speakers must advertise that capability before exchanging EVPN routes.

Four route types are defined:

  • Ethernet Auto-Discovery (type 1): used for fast convergence and for aliasing and backup paths.
  • MAC/IP Advertisement (type 2): tells other PEs that a MAC address, and optionally an IP address, is reachable here, with an MPLS label.
  • Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag (type 3): sets up how broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast traffic reaches this PE.
  • Ethernet Segment (type 4): lets PEs on the same segment discover each other and elect a Designated Forwarder.

Several new extended communities go with them. The ESI Label community (Type 0x06, Sub-Type 0x01) carries a label and a Single-Active flag, the ES-Import Route Target (Sub-Type 0x02) makes only the PEs on a segment import its Ethernet Segment route, the MAC Mobility community (Sub-Type 0x00) carries a sequence number and a sticky flag, and the Default Gateway community marks a gateway MAC address. EVPN routes can carry Route Target attributes, which can be configured or, in the Unique VLAN case, derived from the VLAN ID.
sections.plainLanguage: The routers swap four kinds of notes: here is a cable, here is a computer, here is how to reach me for group messages, and here is a shared cable. Each note has stickers that say how it should be handled.

sections.title: Multihoming: Segments, Forwarders and Aliasing
sections.content:
PEs attached to the same Ethernet segment find each other by exchanging Ethernet Segment routes, which carry an ES-Import Route Target so that only PEs on that segment import them.

For fast convergence, each PE advertises Ethernet A-D per ES routes for each attached segment. If the link to the segment fails, the PE withdraws them, and every remote PE updates the next hops for all MAC addresses on that segment at once, without waiting for each MAC route to be withdrawn.

One PE per VLAN is chosen as the Designated Forwarder (DF) and is the one that sends broadcast and multicast traffic, and flooded unknown unicast, to the CE. The default election is called service carving. A PE advertises its Ethernet Segment route, waits a timer (default value 3 seconds), then sorts the IP addresses of all PEs on the segment. With N PEs, the PE with ordinal i is the DF for VLAN V when V mod N equals i.

For split horizon, a non-DF PE that receives a broadcast, unknown unicast or multicast frame from the CE tags copies of it with an ESI label. When the frame reaches the DF PE for the same segment, that label tells it not to send the frame back to the CE. The label MUST be distributed in an Ethernet A-D per ES route.

For aliasing, a PE can signal with an Ethernet A-D per EVI route that it reaches an EVPN instance on a segment even if it has learned no MAC addresses there. Remote PEs can then load balance over all the PEs on the segment. Segments run in All-Active mode, where all attached PEs forward known unicast traffic, or Single-Active mode, where only one does; the Single-Active flag in the ESI Label community says which.
sections.plainLanguage: If a house has two doors, only one door keeper hands out the group mail so nobody gets two copies. If one door breaks, a single note tells everyone to use the other door right away.

sections.title: Learning MAC Addresses and Answering ARP
sections.content:
A PE MUST support local data-plane learning using standard IEEE Ethernet learning, for example from DHCP requests and ARP requests. It MAY instead learn through the control plane or management plane. Remote learning is done in the control plane: the PE advertises each locally learned MAC address to the other PEs in the EVPN instance in a MAC/IP Advertisement route.

That route holds the Route Distinguisher, the ESI, the Ethernet Tag ID, a MAC address length (set to 48 bits), the MAC address, an optional IP address and one or two MPLS labels. Label1 MUST be downstream assigned. A PE can choose a label per MAC-VRF, per MAC-VRF and Ethernet tag, per ESI and Ethernet tag, or per MAC address. The choice is purely local to the originating PE. A single label per MAC-VRF needs the fewest labels but needs a MAC lookup at the egress PE.

The IP address in the route helps reduce flooding of ARP and Neighbor Discovery messages. When a PE has the MAC binding for an IP address in an ARP Request from a CE, it SHOULD answer on behalf of the owner (ARP proxy). A PE that routes between subnets is the default gateway for the instance and answers ARP Requests for the gateway address itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router keeps a phone book of which computer is behind it and mails its entries to the others. When a computer asks who has a given address, a router that already knows can just answer.

sections.title: Forwarding Unicast and Multi-Destination Traffic
sections.content:
Every PE MUST advertise an Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag route. It carries a Provider Multicast Service Interface (PMSI) Tunnel attribute that says how broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast traffic should be sent to that PE. The PEs can use ingress replication, where the sender makes a copy per remote PE and each copy uses a downstream label, or P2MP LSPs, which are trees built as in RFC 7117.

EVPN does not require PEs to flood unknown unicast. Because MAC addresses are distributed in BGP, they are normally learned before traffic arrives. Flooding is an administrative choice. If it is not allowed, the PE MUST drop packets to unknown MAC addresses.

For a known destination MAC address, the PE sends the frame with the EVPN label advertised by the remote PE for that MAC address, below the LSP label stack needed to reach the remote PE. For a multihomed segment in All-Active mode, a remote PE treats a MAC address as reachable through all PEs that advertised both the Ethernet A-D per ES routes and the Ethernet A-D per EVI route for that segment, and it can load balance across them. In Single-Active mode, the MAC address is reachable only through the PE that advertised it, the primary, and the others serve as backup paths.
sections.plainLanguage: For a package to a known address, the router adds the right label and sends it straight there. For a message to everyone, it either makes a copy for each router or uses one shared path that branches.

sections.title: MAC Mobility, Convergence and Frame Ordering
sections.content:
A host can move from one Ethernet segment to another. The old PEs must withdraw their advertisements for that MAC address. The MAC Mobility extended community carries a sequence number so that all PEs see the latest move. A PE advertising a MAC for the first time sends no community. A PE that sees a MAC that was previously advertised with a different ESI advertises it with a sequence number one greater than the one it received. If two PEs advertise the same sequence number with different ESIs, the route from the PE with the lowest IP address is the best route.

Misconfigured hosts with duplicate MAC addresses could cause endless moves. A PE that detects N MAC moves within an M-second timer (default M = 180, default N = 5) MUST alert the operator and stop sending and processing BGP MAC/IP Advertisement routes for that address until the operator acts. M and N MUST be configurable. A MAC address can also be set as static (sticky), advertised with the static flag set to 1 and sequence number zero.

For convergence, existing MPLS fast reroute can recover from transit link and node failures on the order of 50 ms. A PE failure can be detected from the loss of the BGP session, in the sub-second range if BFD is used. For frame ordering, a destination MAC address whose first nibble is 0x4 or 0x6 can be mistaken for an IP packet by routers that look deep into packets for ECMP. Where that is a risk, the Preferred PW MPLS Control Word with value 0 SHOULD be used over MP2P LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer moves to a new room, it gets a higher version number so everyone trusts the newest address. If two computers fight over one name, the router stops passing the name around and tells a person.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4761 and RFC 4762 apply to MAC learning in the data plane and to flooding, and those of RFC 4364 apply to MAC learning in the control plane over the MPLS/IP core. The control plane is BGP, so techniques such as those in RFC 5925 help authenticate BGP messages and make spoofed updates and withdrawals harder.

Compromise of the control plane could send one customer's data to another EVPN, black-hole it or send it to an eavesdropper. Authentication does not keep MPLS labels private, so someone who knows the labels and has access to the data path could eavesdrop. Users of VPN services are expected to take their own precautions, such as encryption. MPLS labels should be accepted only from valid interfaces, which matters especially for multi-AS EVPN instances.

The duplicate MAC detection of Section 15.1 and the sticky MAC addresses of Section 15.2 help limit malicious traffic from an impostor MAC address.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bad guy could write fake notes in the routers' phone book, mail would go to the wrong place. Routers must check who sent each note, and customers should lock their own mail in an envelope.
